# Modifying Accepted Behavior

The unit-number search from the earlier chapters has already passed review, reached both
repositories, and entered the accepted OpenSpec specification.  Now suppose a product owner asks
for a smaller limit: “Could unit numbers have a maximum of 10 characters instead of requiring 15?”

That request may look like a one-line validation edit.  Adding a second requirement, however,
would leave two current rules for the same input: one requiring 15 characters and another allowing
no more than 10.  Developers, reviewers, and later Copilot sessions would have to guess which one
wins.

OpenSpec treats this situation as a modification.  The change would identify the accepted
requirement, provide its complete replacement, and preserve every scenario that should remain
part of that requirement.  After archive, the main specification should describe one current
rule, without asking readers to reconstruct precedence from change dates.

## Learning objective

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to decide when a request modifies accepted behavior
rather than adding a separate capability.  You should also be able to write a complete
`MODIFIED` requirement, trace its consequences through two repositories, and verify that archive
would leave one coherent source of truth.

## Recognize a replacement

Chapter 12 added VIN search without changing the identity of unit-number search.  VIN introduced a
new way to find a truck, so its requirement could sit beside the accepted unit-number requirement.
The request in this chapter behaves differently.  A unit number cannot remain both exactly 15
characters and at most 10 characters under the same conditions.

Before choosing a delta operation, complete this sentence:

> After this change, the accepted requirement named **Search by unit number** should ...

If the answer begins “still apply, plus users can do something separate,” `ADDED` may fit.  If the
answer begins “mean something different,” `MODIFIED` deserves closer attention.  Removing the
behavior entirely may call for `REMOVED`, while changing only its identity may call for `RENAMED`.

| Question | Likely operation |
|---|---|
| Will a separate requirement coexist with the accepted one? | `ADDED` |
| Will the accepted requirement keep its identity but change meaning? | `MODIFIED` |
| Will the accepted requirement cease to apply? | `REMOVED` |
| Will its identity change while its intended behavior remains? | `RENAMED` |

Implementation files cannot settle this choice on their own.  Two validators might share a helper
even though they implement separate requirements, while one requirement might span an API,
generated client, form, and several tests.  The operation follows the relationship between
accepted and proposed behavior, not the number or shape of files involved.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A newer sentence does not cancel an older requirement

Appending “Unit numbers SHALL contain no more than 10 characters” under `ADDED Requirements` would
leave the accepted 15-character rule in force.  Neither recency nor proximity supplies replacement
semantics.  Use `MODIFIED` when review intends one requirement to supersede its accepted version.
:::

## Recover the accepted baseline

Before drafting a replacement, inspect the requirement as it exists under `openspec/specs/`.
Record its heading exactly, along with every scenario nested beneath it.  OpenSpec uses that
requirement identity when applying the delta, and those scenarios reveal behavior that a short
change request might otherwise erase.

For the lab, the baseline investigation might ask:

- Does the requirement say exactly 15 characters, or no more than 15?
- Does it describe trimming or another form of normalization?
- Which cases cover matching, no match, empty input, and invalid input?
- Do the backend and frontend specifications express the same boundary?
- Which tests provide evidence for each accepted scenario?

A small baseline table can keep evidence separate from decisions:

| Topic | Accepted source | Implementation evidence | Decision needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length rule | Main unit-number specification | Backend and frontend boundary tests | Yes, replace 15 with the reviewed rule |
| Normalization | Accepted scenarios, if present | Controller, form, and tests | Only if the request leaves it unclear |
| Empty input | Accepted scenarios, if present | Validation tests | Only if the new meaning could differ |
| Match and no match | Accepted scenarios | Service, component, and browser tests | Usually preserve unless scope says otherwise |

If the specification, code, and tests disagree, record the mismatch as a review finding.  Do not
choose whichever behavior is easiest to edit.  The team may resolve the mismatch inside this
change when it affects the revised rule, or record separate work when it does not.  Either choice
should remain visible in the proposal.

## Separate the request from its unanswered questions

“Maximum of 10 characters” answers less than it first appears to.  Before proposal, the team still
needs to decide:

- whether values shorter than 10 characters qualify;
- whether normalization occurs before the length check;
- how the system handles empty and oversized values; and
- whether case handling, matching, and no-match behavior change with the boundary.

An exploration prompt could make those gaps visible before proposal begins:

```markdown
/opsx:explore

We are considering changing the accepted unit-number rule from 15 characters to a maximum of 10.

Please identify:
- the accepted requirement and all of its scenarios;
- every backend and frontend boundary that represents the current length rule;
- generated files and contracts affected by the rule;
- behaviors the request does not settle, including normalization and empty input; and
- tests that provide evidence for behavior likely to remain unchanged.

Do not modify files or infer product decisions from the current implementation.
```

Organize the resulting notes by what changes, what remains, and what still needs a decision:

| Category | Example | Treatment in the change |
|---|---|---|
| Requested difference | Replace the 15-character rule with a maximum of 10 | State in the proposal and delta |
| Preserved behavior | A valid value with no match keeps the accepted no-match outcome | Restate its scenario in the replacement requirement |
| Open decision | Whether trimming occurs before the length check | Resolve before apply or mark as blocking |

This separation adds a review step before coding.  It also exposes disagreements before the
backend and Angular repositories implement different interpretations.

## Write the proposal around the behavioral change

Once review settles the open questions, the proposal can state both the intended difference and
the preservation boundary.  For this worked example, suppose the team chooses these exercise
assumptions:

- leading and trailing spaces are removed before validation;
- one through 10 remaining characters are valid;
- an empty value remains invalid;
- 11 or more remaining characters are invalid;
- matching remains exact; and
- a valid value with no match returns no matching trucks.

Those are example product decisions, not consequences of the word `MODIFIED`.  Another team might
choose different answers and still use the same OpenSpec operation.

A compact proposal could read:

```markdown
# Change: Reduce the unit-number length limit

## Why

The business now assigns unit numbers containing between one and 10 characters.  The search still
requires exact matching after removing leading and trailing spaces.

## What Changes

- Remove leading and trailing spaces before validating the unit number.
- Accept between one and 10 remaining characters.
- Reject empty values and values longer than 10 characters.
- Preserve exact matching and the existing no-match result.
- Publish the revised constraint through the backend-owned OpenAPI contract.

## Non-Goals

- Changes to VIN search
- Partial or fuzzy unit-number matching
- New result fields or response states
```

Naming unchanged behavior limits the change.  A length edit can invite nearby cleanup or a new
matching strategy, but the non-goals and preservation claims give reviewers a boundary for those
edits without copying unrelated specifications into the delta.

## Replace the complete requirement

A `MODIFIED` section should contain the whole requirement as it ought to read after archive.  It
should not contain a patch fragment such as “change 15 to 10,” because that fragment would depend
on a reader finding and mentally merging the accepted version.

Using the exercise assumptions, a backend delta might look like this:

```markdown
## MODIFIED Requirements

### Requirement: Search by unit number

The API SHALL remove leading and trailing spaces from a unit-number search value.  The remaining
value SHALL contain between one and 10 characters, and the API SHALL match it exactly against unit
numbers.

#### Scenario: Matching unit number is at the maximum length

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRUCK-1234`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-1234`
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Matching unit number is shorter than the maximum

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRK-123`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRK-123`
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Matching unit number has surrounding spaces

- **GIVEN** a truck has unit number `TRUCK-1234`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `  TRUCK-1234  `
- **THEN** the API returns that truck

#### Scenario: Unit number exceeds the maximum

- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-12345`
- **THEN** the API rejects the search value as invalid

#### Scenario: Unit number is empty

- **WHEN** a client searches with a value that is empty after removing surrounding spaces
- **THEN** the API rejects the search value as invalid

#### Scenario: No truck matches

- **GIVEN** no truck has unit number `TRUCK-9999`
- **WHEN** a client searches for `TRUCK-9999`
- **THEN** the API returns no matching trucks
```

This example is complete only under the stated exercise assumptions.  Compare it with the actual
lab requirement before using it.  If that requirement contains another match, failure, or response
scenario, carry the scenario forward unless the proposal deliberately changes or removes it.

The requirement heading deserves special care.  If the accepted heading reads `Search by unit
number`, changing it casually to `Validate a unit number` may prevent a clean identity match or
misrepresent the requirement's scope.  Copy the accepted heading, then revise the body and
scenarios beneath it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Complete does not mean duplicated

Completeness applies to the requirement being replaced.  The delta need not copy every requirement
in the capability, nor should it repeat unrelated VIN behavior.  Include the revised requirement
and all scenarios that should survive within that requirement.
:::

## Inspect the delta before implementation

OpenSpec validation can catch malformed delta structure, while a behavioral diff can expose an
accidental deletion or an unchanged 15-character clause.  Run the repository's configured checks,
then inspect the proposed difference:

```bash
openspec validate reduce-unit-number-limit --strict
openspec show reduce-unit-number-limit --diff
```

Review the diff against these checks:

- Match the modified heading to the accepted requirement.
- Confirm that archive would replace the 15-character wording rather than retain it beside the
	new rule.
- Account for every scenario named by the proposal.
- Remove implementation choices, such as Java annotations or Angular validators, from the
	behavioral specification.
- Confirm that each boundary scenario could fail for the intended reason before implementation.

A passing structural check cannot answer all of those questions.  Human review still needs to
judge whether the replacement captures the business decision and whether its preservation claims
are credible.

## Trace one rule through two repositories

The modified requirement may be small, but the old constraint may have crossed several ownership
boundaries.  Search for the old value and for the concepts that express it.  A literal search for
`15` could find noise and miss a named constant, a schema facet, or prose that says “fifteen,” so
combine value searches with searches for requirement names, validation messages, and test cases.

| Boundary | What may need review | What would count as drift? |
|---|---|---|
| Backend request validation | Length annotation, validator, or request parsing | API still accepts 11 through 15 characters |
| Search behavior | Service and persistence tests | Matching changes even though the proposal preserves it |
| OpenAPI document | `maxLength`, descriptions, and responses | Published schema still advertises 15 |
| Generated Angular client | Regenerated request types or metadata | Hand edit disappears on regeneration |
| Angular form | Validators, feedback, and submission state | UI rejects a valid 10-character value or accepts 11 |
| Visible text | Labels, hints, and errors | User sees the obsolete limit |
| Automated tests | Boundary and preserved-behavior cases | Tests prove only the new happy path |

The backend should continue to own the wire contract.  After its validation and OpenAPI output
reflect the reviewed delta, inspect the contract diff before regenerating the Angular client.  Form
tests and UI changes may proceed against the reviewed frontend delta, but client integration
should wait for the backend-owned contract if generation is the established handoff.

Avoid editing generated client files as though they owned the rule.  A manual fix could make the
current branch compile, yet regeneration would restore whatever the OpenAPI document still says.
The durable correction belongs in the source contract and generation workflow.

## Apply in an order that preserves evidence

A task list might keep the dependency visible without prescribing every class or function:

1. Add or revise backend tests for 10-character, shorter valid, 11-character, and empty values.
2. Update backend validation while preserving accepted match, no-match, and error behavior.
3. Generate and review the OpenAPI document for the revised constraint and unrelated drift.
4. Regenerate the Angular client from the reviewed contract.
5. Update Angular validation, visible feedback, and focused component tests.
6. Exercise the integrated path and rerun preserved-behavior tests in both repositories.

Begin with boundary evidence.  A test for exactly 10 characters and another for 11 can show whether
the implementation changed the intended edge rather than merely replacing one constant.  Tests
for matching and no match then check the proposal's claim that the rest of the search behavior
survived.

During apply, ask Copilot to work from scenario names and report the evidence for each one.  A
message such as “updated max length everywhere” would reveal little about normalization, generated
artifacts, or regression coverage.  A scenario-to-test trace gives the reviewer something more
specific to inspect.

## Verify the replacement before archive

Verification has two jobs: show that the implementation adopted the new boundary and show that the
change preserved everything it claimed not to alter.

| Claim | Focused evidence |
|---|---|
| A normalized 10-character value is accepted | Backend boundary test and Angular form test |
| A normalized value shorter than 10 is accepted | Backend and frontend validation tests |
| An 11-character value is rejected | API validation test and visible-feedback test |
| Empty input follows the reviewed rule | Backend and Angular empty-input tests |
| Match and no-match behavior remain intact | Existing service, component, and integrated tests |
| Both repositories share the revised contract | Reviewed OpenAPI diff and generated-client diff |
| The old rule no longer survives | Search across specs, code, generated output, tests, and UI text |

Run focused checks first, then the broader repository suites and integrated path.  If an
11-character value fails in the UI but reaches the backend through another path, the replacement
has not reached every boundary.  If all tests pass while the generated schema still reports 15,
the repositories still disagree about their contract.

Before archive, inspect the source-of-truth result that synchronization would produce.  Confirm
that the main specification would contain one complete unit-number requirement with the
10-character maximum and every preserved scenario.  If understanding the current rule still
requires an older archived change, the active delta remains incomplete.

After archive, repeat the obsolete-assumption search against the main specification and generated
artifacts.  The dated change record may retain the old rule as history; the active source of truth
should not present it as current behavior.

## Hands-on exercise

Use the two lab repositories to propose, apply, verify, and archive the revised unit-number rule.
Keep a compact record that another reviewer could follow without replaying the Copilot chat:

```text
Product change: reduce-unit-number-limit
Accepted requirement: Search by unit number
Old rule: <exact accepted wording>
Reviewed replacement: <exact revised wording>
Preserved scenarios: <scenario names>
Open questions: <owners and blocking status>
Backend evidence: <commands and results>
Contract evidence: <OpenAPI and generated-client diffs>
Frontend evidence: <commands and results>
Post-archive search: <obsolete assumptions found or none>
```

Pause when exploration exposes an unanswered product decision.  Revise the delta after that
decision receives review, then resume implementation from the updated scenarios.  A code-only
choice or a corrective chat message would leave the next agent with the same ambiguity.

## Verification checkpoint

The change may be ready to close when the modified heading matches the accepted requirement, the
delta supplies its complete replacement, and strict validation passes.  Focused tests should cover
both sides of the new boundary, while regression evidence should cover the scenarios promised as
unchanged.  The OpenAPI and generated-client diffs should describe the same maximum, and a search
should find no current 15-character assumption outside historical records.

If one of those checks fails, keep the change open.  Update the artifact that owns the discrepancy,
repeat the narrow check, and inspect the would-be source of truth again before archive.

## What you learned

`MODIFIED` means supplying the exact requirement that should exist after archive, not editing only
the sentence that changed.  Archive can preserve only the scenarios present in that replacement,
so an omitted scenario changes the source of truth whether the omission was deliberate or not.
